chunks: Muhammad ibn Yahya, from al-'Amraki ibn 'Ali, from 'Ali ibn Ja'far عليه السلام, who said:

I asked him about a man who slaughtered a sheep, then it convulsed and fell into a well of water while its veins were gushing blood. Can wudu (ablution) be performed from that well? He said: "Between thirty and forty buckets are to be drawn from it, then wudu (ablution) may be performed from it, and there is no harm in it."

He said: And I asked him about a man who slaughtered a chicken or a pigeon and it fell into a well. Is it proper to perform wudu (ablution) from it? He said: "A few buckets are to be drawn from it, then wudu (ablution) may be performed from it."
And I asked him about a man drawing water from a well, then his nose bled into it. Can wudu (ablution) be performed from it? He said: "A few buckets are to be drawn from it."

key_terms.بِئْرِ: a well from which water is drawn
key_terms.دَلْوًا: a bucket used for drawing water
key_terms.لَا بَأْسَ بِهِ: there is no harm in it; it is permissible
key_terms.يَتَوَضَّأُ: to perform wudu (ablution) using the water
key_terms.يُنْزَحُ: water is to be drawn out from the well

ai.seo_question: How many buckets should be drawn from a well if blood falls into it before performing wudu (ablution)?
ai.summary: This hadith gives legal rulings regarding well water when contaminated by blood from a slaughtered animal or by nosebleed. It specifies the amount of water to be drawn out before the water may be used again for wudu (ablution), showing practical rulings of ritual purity in cases of impurity affecting wells.
